c: Pinewood Print Works, a print shop with 14 employees that makes posters, banners and school yearbooks
s: Over the past year Pinewood lost three of its five best press operators to a competitor that pays about 8 percent more. Yearbook orders now arrive late four times out of ten, and two school customers have said they may not renew. The owner wants to stop the turnover without hurting profit.
The owner (judge) can raise total wage spending by no more than 5 percent and has asked you to find the real problem, weigh the options, and recommend a plan with a way to tell whether it works.
You have 7 minutes to explain your analysis, the alternatives you considered with the pros and cons of each, and your recommendation.
f: Annual payroll: $620,000; maximum increase allowed: 5% ($31,000)
Turnover: 3 of 5 senior press operators left in 12 months
Late orders: 40% of yearbook jobs; the two at-risk schools represent $96,000 in yearly sales
Exit interviews mention pay, last-minute overtime and no path to a lead role
Replacing a press operator costs about $14,000 in hiring and training
n: Separates symptoms (late orders) from causes (turnover, scheduling, no career path)
Weighs at least three alternatives, such as a raise, a lead-operator role and better scheduling, with pros and cons
Shows the plan fits inside the $31,000 limit with real numbers
Compares the cost of turnover (about $42,000 so far) with the cost of retention
Describes implementation steps and who is responsible for each
Proposes measures for six months, such as turnover, on-time rate and renewals
q: Why not just match the competitor's pay?
How would you decide who gets the lead operator role?
What would you do if the late orders continue after three months?

c: Crescent Foods, a regional maker of frozen meals sold in 120 grocery stores
s: Crescent Foods has had two supplier problems in six months. Its only tray supplier shipped three weeks late and forced a production halt, and a produce supplier delivered a batch that failed a quality check. Production stopped for a total of 9 days, costing the company roughly $180,000 in lost sales.

The vice president of operations (judge) wants to reduce this risk. The options are to find a second supplier for trays, to buy a larger safety stock of trays, or to move to a supplier-quality program with audits. Each option costs money and affects other parts of the supply chain.
You have 7 minutes to explain how a supply chain problem like this affects performance, compare the options, and recommend a plan.
f: Lost sales from the two incidents: about $180,000
Tray supply: one supplier provides 100% of trays; a second supplier charges 6% more per tray
Safety stock option: holding six extra weeks of trays would cost about $22,000 in storage and tied-up cash
Quality audit program: about $30,000 per year
Annual tray spending: $410,000
n: Explains the supply chain and how a single point of failure affects performance
Compares a second supplier, safety stock and an audit program, with costs and trade-offs for each
Estimates the added cost of a second supplier (about $24,600 a year if all trays moved, less if split)
Recommends a combination and explains how it reduces risk for less than the loss
Mentions quality management and risk management
Describes how to measure success, such as on-time delivery and production days lost
q: Is it worth paying more for a supplier we might not use much?
How would you phase in your recommendation?
What is the downside of holding a large inventory of trays?

c: BrightPath Learning Center, an after-school tutoring business with four locations and 36 employees
s: BrightPath's tutors work part time and about half leave within a year. Parents say they value consistency, and the CEO believes the turnover is hurting renewals. A recent survey found that tutors want clearer expectations, regular feedback and a chance to earn more as they gain experience.

The CEO (judge) wants a plan that improves retention but cannot increase total labor costs by more than $18,000 per year. The CEO is considering three ideas: a tutor career ladder with pay steps, a mentoring program that pairs new tutors with experienced ones, and a monthly bonus tied to student progress.
You have 7 minutes to explain which people-management factors matter here, the alternatives with pros and cons, and your recommendation.
f: 36 employees, 28 of them part-time tutors
Tutor turnover: 52% a year; family renewals: 71%
Average cost to recruit and train a tutor: $1,300
Labor budget increase limit: $18,000 per year
Survey: 64% of tutors want clearer expectations; 58% want feedback; 41% mention pay
n: Applies human resources management basics: onboarding, feedback, development and pay
Calculates the cost of turnover (about 15 tutors a year, near $19,500) and compares it with the $18,000 limit
Weighs the career ladder, mentoring and bonus options with pros and cons
Recommends a specific mix and shows it fits the budget
Explains how change management will help staff accept new expectations
Names measures such as turnover, renewals and satisfaction
q: Why not just raise everyone's pay?
How would mentoring work when mentors are also part time?
Which measure will you check first, and when?

c: Redwood Cycles, a bike shop and repair business with two stores
s: Redwood Cycles had record sales this year, but the owner is surprised that the bank balance is low. Profit on the income statement is $48,000, yet the shop had to delay paying two suppliers last month. The owner wants to understand what is going on before deciding whether to open a third store next spring.

The owner (judge) has handed you the latest income statement, balance sheet and cash flow information and asked you to explain the gap between profit and cash, the options for improving cash, and whether a third store is wise right now.
You have 7 minutes to give your analysis and recommendation.
f: Net income: $48,000; cash balance: $9,500
Inventory grew from $120,000 to $210,000 over the year
Accounts payable due within 30 days: $64,000
A third store would cost about $150,000 to open
Cash flow from operations: negative $22,000; the owner funded part of the shortfall with a $30,000 line of credit
n: Explains why profit and cash differ: inventory growth, payables and timing
Reads the balance sheet, income statement and cash flow statement correctly
Gives alternatives, such as reducing inventory, negotiating supplier terms or a longer credit line, with pros and cons
Advises on the third store with reasons, probably waiting until cash flow improves
Provides a simple budget or cash plan for the next six months
Names measures such as inventory turnover and the cash balance
q: Why is inventory such a big part of the problem?
What would you tell the suppliers we have not paid?
Under what conditions would you say yes to the third store?

c: Coastal Craft Brewing, a local craft brewery planning to sell in neighboring states
s: Coastal Craft Brewing sells its beer in 40 local restaurants and its taproom. A distributor has offered to carry the beer in two neighboring states, which would raise sales by an estimated 35 percent. Alcohol sales are regulated differently in each state, taxes vary, and the brewery's current staff already works near capacity.

The general manager (judge) wants to know whether to accept the distributor's offer, expand more slowly, or stay local. The brewery must consider legal rules, the competitive environment, its organization and its resources.
You have 7 minutes to explain the issues, compare the alternatives with pros and cons, and recommend a decision.
f: Current annual sales: $1.4 million; the expansion could add about $490,000 a year
Brewery capacity: it already runs at 90% of production capacity
Adding a fermentation tank would cost about $85,000
State licensing and tax rules differ; each new state needs a separate distributor license
Craft beer is competitive in both neighboring states, with at least 12 established local breweries
n: Identifies legal and regulatory issues affecting the expansion
Discusses the competitive and economic environment in the new states
Compares at least three options (full expansion, phased expansion, stay local) with pros and cons
Considers capacity and the investment needed, including the tank
Recommends a specific path and sets milestones
Mentions how the organization's design and staffing must change
q: What is the biggest risk in saying yes to the distributor?
How would you decide which of the two states to enter first?
What would make you change your recommendation?
